findings.title: Team admins are rejected by the authorization check
findings.body: The code combines `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner` with `&&`. A team administrator who is not also the owner will therefore fail this check, even though the UI and variable name indicate that either role should be permitted. This prevents team admins from adding guests to bookings they are authorized to manage; use an OR check for the two roles.

findings.title: The mutation adds attendees to bookings in invalid states
findings.body: After verifying only that the booking exists, the handler persists new attendees without checking booking status. Although the UI hides the action for cancelled, rejected, and pending bookings, any authenticated attendee/organizer can invoke this tRPC mutation directly for those bookings. The handler then updates the calendar and sends invitations whose ICS status is CONFIRMED, effectively inviting people to an event that may be cancelled or never accepted.

findings.title: Calendar updates use the guest's credentials rather than the booking owner's
findings.body: Attendees are explicitly allowed to add guests, but the EventManager is initialized with credentials loaded for `ctx.user`, i.e. the attendee performing the action. The destination calendar and event references normally belong to `booking.user` (whose credentials were already loaded in the booking query). A permitted attendee generally cannot update the organizer's calendar, so the local attendee rows are created but the organizer's calendar event cannot be updated.

findings.title: Local attendee records are committed before the external calendar update succeeds
findings.body: `prisma.booking.update` permanently creates the attendee rows before `updateCalendarAttendees` is called. If the calendar provider update throws, the mutation fails after the database has changed, leaving Cal.com and the external event with different attendee lists. Retrying the same request then finds no `uniqueGuests` and returns BAD_REQUEST instead of retrying the calendar update. This needs compensating cleanup or a durable/outbox-based retry strategy.

findings.title: The server accepts duplicate guest addresses in a single request
findings.body: The tRPC input schema does not require unique guests, and this filter only compares each submitted address against attendees that existed before the update. A direct request such as `guests: ["guest@example.com", "guest@example.com"]` leaves both values in `uniqueGuests` and passes them to `createMany`, resulting in duplicate attendee records (or a database constraint failure if such a constraint is present). Client-side validation is not sufficient for this API boundary.

findings.title: Blacklist matching can be bypassed with email capitalization
findings.body: Configured blacklisted addresses are normalized to lowercase, but submitted guest addresses are compared without normalization. `BLOCKED@example.com` passes Zod validation and does not match a blacklist entry of `blocked@example.com`, allowing callers to bypass the explicit guest-email blocklist. Normalize/canonicalize the submitted email before checking the blacklist and existing attendees.

findings.title: Existing attendees can receive a new-booking email when mixed with new guests
findings.body: The database correctly filters existing addresses into `uniqueGuests`, but email classification receives the original `guests` input. For example, submitting an existing attendee plus one new address creates only the new attendee, yet `sendAddGuestsEmails` treats the existing attendee as newly added and sends them `AttendeeScheduledEmail` rather than the guest-added notification. Pass the successfully added `uniqueGuests` list to avoid false scheduling emails.

findings.title: Add-guest notifications ignore event email-disable settings
findings.body: `sendAddGuestsEmails` has no event metadata argument and unconditionally queues organizer and attendee emails. Other standard booking email paths check `disableStandardEmails` through `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` and `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`. Consequently, adding a guest sends notifications despite the event type being configured to suppress host or attendee standard emails.

findings.title: Team members are never included in add-guest notifications
findings.body: The constructed `CalendarEvent` never sets its `team` field. As a result, the `calendarEvent.team?.members` branch in `sendAddGuestsEmails` is always skipped, even though the mailer explicitly attempts to notify team members. For team bookings, only the assigned organizer receives the notification and the rest of the team is silently omitted.
